common_name: Belinda's Dream Rose (Texas Earth-Kind Landscape Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Belinda's Dream was bred in Texas and earned Earth-Kind rose status from Texas A&M for its outstanding heat tolerance and disease resistance without spraying.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Belinda's Dream needs little more than an occasional deep watering once established. Bred in Texas and one of the first roses awarded Earth-Kind status by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, a designation reserved for roses proven to thrive in Southern heat and humidity with minimal fertilizer, spraying, or supplemental water, Belinda's Dream produces large, fully double, clear pink, classically shaped blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance in continuous flushes from spring through frost. Its excellent resistance to black spot and powdery mildew makes it dependable in the humid Gulf South where many hybrid tea roses struggle without a regular spray program, and the vigorous, upright shrub works equally well as a specimen, a hedge, or a source of cut flowers. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new growth and the best bloom production.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Earth-Kind Roses

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Perle d'Or is an 1884 French polyantha, often compared to the similar Cecile Brunner, valued for clusters of small, apricot-pink, old-fashioned blooms on a tough, easygoing shrub.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Perle d'Or needs little beyond an occasional deep watering once it's established. Introduced in France in 1884, Perle d'Or is a classic polyantha rose closely related to the better-known Cecile Brunner, producing abundant clusters of small, high-centered, apricot-to-golden-pink blooms with a spicy-sweet fragrance held above neat, small foliage on a tough, twiggy shrub. It blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through frost, tolerates poor soil and Southern heat and humidity with minimal disease trouble, and its small flower size and clustered habit make it an excellent choice for cutting or for a low, informal hedge. Prune back by about a third in late winter to shape the shrub and encourage vigorous new growth loaded with flower buds.

common_name: Reve d'Or Rose (Golden Buff Antique Noisette Climber)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring near a fence, trellis, or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun; Reve d'Or is an 1869 French Noisette climber, a class of rose bred in the American South, valued for warm golden-buff blooms and strong heat tolerance.

directions: Plant near a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained, average soil in full sun, and tie in the long canes horizontally as they grow to encourage more flowering laterals along their length. Reve d'Or, French for golden dream, is a nineteenth-century Noisette climbing rose, a class first developed in Charleston, South Carolina and especially well adapted to Southern heat and humidity, producing large, cupped, warm buff-to-golden-apricot blooms with a fruity fragrance in flushes from spring through fall. Its glossy, reddish-tinted new foliage and relatively thornless, vigorous canes make it a forgiving climber for training over an arbor or along a fence, and it tolerates the Gulf Coast growing season with far less disease trouble than modern climbing hybrid teas. Prune out only dead or crossing wood in late winter, since Noisettes bloom best on older, well-established wood left largely undisturbed.

common_name: Maggie Rose (Found Texas China-Bourbon Antique Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Maggie is a found rose rediscovered growing at old Texas homesites, believed to be a China-Bourbon hybrid, valued for rich magenta-pink, cupped, fragrant blooms on a tough, low-care shrub.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Maggie needs little beyond an occasional deep watering once established. Like many of the antique roses preserved through the Texas rose rustling movement, Maggie is a found rose, rediscovered growing untended at an old homestead and propagated from cuttings rather than traced to a known breeder or introduction date, and it is generally considered a China-Bourbon hybrid based on its growth habit and bloom. It produces richly fragrant, cupped, deep magenta-pink flowers in generous flushes from spring through fall on a vigorous, well-branched shrub that shrugs off Southern heat, humidity, and poor soil with the same toughness that let it survive decades of neglect at its original homesite. Its resilience and near-constant bloom make it an excellent low-input choice for a Gulf Coast heirloom border, and it asks for little beyond an occasional shaping prune after the heaviest spring flush.
